body:
DNA carries hereditary information

Organisms resemble their parents because biological information is passed from one generation to the next. In most organisms this information is carried by deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). DNA also helps direct the activities of a living cell. It is not the same thing as a protein: DNA stores instructions, while proteins perform many of the structural and chemical functions needed by cells.

DNA is a long molecule made of repeating units called nucleotides. Each nucleotide contains a sugar called deoxyribose, a phosphate group and 1 nitrogenous base.

The 4 bases in DNA are adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). In the usual double-stranded DNA molecule, the 2 chains form a double helix. Their bases pair specifically: A pairs with T and G pairs with C. A–T pairs have 2 hydrogen bonds and G–C pairs have 3. The order of bases along a strand carries information; the pairing rule allows each strand to serve as a guide when DNA is copied.

How genes, chromosomes and genomes are related

In human, animal and plant cells, most DNA is present in the nucleus, packaged with proteins into chromosomes. A gene is a functional unit of heredity: usually a defined DNA sequence whose information is used to produce a functional RNA or protein. A chromosome contains many genes and other DNA sequences. The genome is the complete set of genetic material of an organism; it is not merely the collection of protein-coding genes.

Alternative forms of a gene are called alleles. They may differ in DNA sequence and can help explain variation in a characteristic. A change in DNA sequence is a mutation or genetic variant, but not every such change causes a visible trait or disease. Traits can also be influenced by the environment and by several genes acting together.

Important locations and numbers

A typical human body cell contains 46 nuclear chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs; a normal human sperm or egg contains 23 nuclear chromosomes. Bacteria have no membrane-bound nucleus; their main DNA lies in a region called the nucleoid. DNA also occurs in mitochondria and, in plants, chloroplasts. Some viruses, unlike cellular organisms, use RNA rather than DNA as their genetic material.

Replication means making a copy of DNA, normally before cell division. Replication preserves genetic information by using the A–T and G–C pairing rules. It differs from the production of RNA or protein from a gene.

Prelims focus

  • DNA bases: A, T, G and C; complementary pairs: A–T and G–C.
  • A DNA nucleotide contains deoxyribose, phosphate and a base.
  • A gene is a functional DNA unit; a genome is the complete genetic set.
  • Human body cells ordinarily have 46 nuclear chromosomes; gametes have 23.
  • Bacterial DNA is not enclosed by a true nucleus.
  • Trap: Not every part of DNA is a protein-coding gene, and not every genetic change causes disease.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, “The Fundamental Unit of Life”, §5.2.3, printed p. 62 (GPSC Books vol. 31, PDF p. 63); NCERT, Biology, Class 12, “Molecular Basis of Inheritance”, §6.1 (GPSC Books vol. 35, PDF pp. 98–102); US National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), “Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) Fact Sheet”, sections “What is DNA made of?” and “What does DNA do?” (consulted 5 November 2026).]

title: DNA, genes and chromosomes: where hereditary information is stored

body:
DNA and RNA are related but not identical

Ribonucleic acid (RNA) is another nucleic acid built from nucleotides. RNA usually has 1 strand, contains the sugar ribose and uses uracil (U) instead of thymine. DNA is generally more stable for long-term information storage; RNA performs several jobs in using, carrying and regulating genetic information.

FeatureDNARNA
SugarDeoxyriboseRibose
BasesA, T, G, CA, U, G, C
Usual structureDouble-stranded helixSingle-stranded
Main cellular roleRelatively stable genetic storeMessages, protein-making machinery and regulation

Replication, transcription and translation do different jobs

Before a cell divides, DNA replication copies its genetic material so new cells can inherit it. When a cell needs a gene product, it can instead use transcription: an enzyme makes an RNA copy from a selected DNA region. In RNA, U pairs with A while the copy is formed. This is not duplication of the entire genome.

For a protein-coding gene, the resulting messenger RNA (mRNA) carries the coded information to a ribosome, where translation builds a protein from amino acids. The message is read in groups of 3 RNA bases, called codons. A protein's amino-acid sequence affects its shape and function, helping explain how a DNA sequence can influence a characteristic.

Three common types of RNA

  • mRNA (messenger RNA): conveys the information for making a protein.
  • tRNA (transfer RNA): brings the appropriate amino acids to the ribosome during translation.
  • rRNA (ribosomal RNA): forms an important structural and functional part of ribosomes.

Some genes produce functional RNA instead of a protein. Moreover, cells do not express all their genes at the same level all the time. For example, the insulin gene is active in the appropriate pancreatic cells, while other cells may carry that gene without making significant amounts of insulin. Gene expression describes how information in a gene is used to produce its functional product; whether and how strongly a gene is expressed depends on the cell and conditions.

The familiar information flow is DNA to RNA to protein for protein-coding genes, but it has qualifications. Not all genes encode proteins; RNA can itself be the final product. Certain viruses have RNA genomes, and retroviruses can make DNA from RNA by reverse transcription.

Prelims focus

  • RNA contains ribose and uracil; DNA contains deoxyribose and thymine.
  • Replication copies DNA; transcription makes RNA using DNA information.
  • Translation occurs at ribosomes and produces a polypeptide or protein.
  • mRNA carries the message, tRNA brings amino acids and rRNA is part of the ribosome.
  • A codon consists of 3 RNA bases.
  • Trap: Gene expression is not another name for DNA replication.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, “Molecular Basis of Inheritance”, §§6.1, 6.4–6.7 (GPSC Books vol. 35, PDF pp. 98–118); NHGRI, “Ribonucleic Acid (RNA)” and “Gene Expression”, Talking Glossary of Genetic Terms, definition sections (consulted 5 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Replication copies DNA; transcription makes RNA from a selected gene; ribosomes translate mRNA into protein. Retroviruses reverse-transcribe RNA into DNA.
pictures.caption: Replicating DNA, transcribing RNA and translating protein are different processes.

title: DNA and RNA: how a gene is expressed

body:
What biotechnology and recombinant DNA mean

Biotechnology uses living organisms, cells or biological components to make useful products or carry out useful tasks. Traditional practices such as making curd or bread use microorganisms without deliberately rearranging genes. Modern biotechnology can go further by using recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology to bring selected DNA sequences together in combinations that were not originally linked. The sequences may come from different organisms, but this is not essential to every recombinant DNA construct.

Recombinant DNA is DNA formed by joining or rearranging selected DNA segments. Genetic engineering deliberately changes genetic material to obtain a desired characteristic or biological product. The aim is to use or modify biological instructions, not merely to observe them.

Why different biological tools are useful

At the conceptual level, different tools have distinct purposes. Restriction endonucleases recognise particular DNA sequences and cut DNA. DNA ligase joins DNA fragments. A vector, such as a bacterial plasmid, can carry a selected DNA segment into a suitable host cell. Plasmids are DNA molecules that can replicate independently of the main bacterial chromosome. Under suitable biological conditions, the host can copy the introduced DNA and may express its information to produce a protein.

The useful outcome depends on what gene has been introduced and whether it functions in that host. Merely inserting a DNA fragment does not guarantee that it will be expressed, produce an effective protein or create the intended characteristic. A host carrying an introduced gene is not the same as the isolated recombinant DNA molecule.

Two clear examples

Human insulin produced using microorganisms

The gene information for human insulin can be used in genetically engineered microorganisms to make insulin for medical use. The microorganism is a producer of the protein; it is not the source of the human insulin gene. Recombinant insulin is an example of manufacturing a useful biological product, not a method of diagnosing diabetes.

Insect-resistant crops

Genes from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis can be introduced into cotton plants so that the plants produce particular Bt (Cry) proteins active against certain insect pests, notably susceptible cotton bollworms. This gives a crop a specific protective trait. It does not make the crop resistant to every insect, every plant disease or drought. Resistance also depends on the pest and the Bt protein involved.

Recombinant DNA technology changes or combines DNA for a purpose. PCR copies a selected DNA region, and sequencing reads the order of its bases. The 3 methods can support one another but are not interchangeable.

Prelims focus

  • Restriction endonuclease: cuts DNA at recognised sites.
  • DNA ligase: joins DNA fragments.
  • Plasmid: a commonly used DNA carrier or vector.
  • Recombinant insulin: a therapeutic protein produced using engineered cells.
  • Bt cotton: a crop with insect-resistance genes derived from Bacillus thuringiensis.
  • Trap: Recombinant DNA does not mean PCR amplification, and Bt cotton is not resistant to all pests.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, “Biotechnology: Principles and Processes”, §§11.1–11.3 (GPSC Books vol. 35, PDF pp. 218–230); NCERT, Biology, Class 12, “Biotechnology and its Applications”, §§12.1–12.2.1 (GPSC Books vol. 35, PDF pp. 232–236); NHGRI, “Recombinant DNA Technology”, Talking Glossary of Genetic Terms, definition (consulted 5 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: A plasmid carries human insulin gene information into an engineered bacterium, whose expression produces insulin for purification and medical use.
pictures.caption: Recombinant DNA can enable host cells to make a useful protein such as human insulin.

title: Recombinant DNA: using genetic information to make useful products

body:
Why a small DNA sample can be tested

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a method for making many copies of a specific DNA segment. When a target sequence occurs in very small amounts, repeated copying makes it easier to detect or study. PCR therefore uses the natural principle of complementary base pairing, but its objective is narrower than the replication of a cell's entire genome.

Short pieces of DNA called primers identify the region to be copied, and a DNA polymerase makes new DNA strands using existing DNA as a guide. Repeated rounds of copying amplify the chosen region. The important idea is selective amplification: PCR does not automatically multiply every DNA molecule present equally, nor does it read out the entire sequence of the product.

How tests work when the original material is RNA

Standard PCR amplifies DNA. For an RNA target, such as genetic material from an RNA virus, the RNA is first converted into complementary DNA (cDNA) by reverse transcriptase. The DNA copy can then be amplified. This combined approach is reverse-transcription PCR (RT-PCR).

MethodWhat happensBasic purpose
PCRCopies a specified DNA segmentFind or study DNA targets
RT-PCRConverts RNA to DNA, then amplifies itFind or study RNA targets
Real-time PCR (qPCR)Monitors amplification as it happensDetect and estimate the amount of a target

Tests can combine the ideas: real-time RT-PCR is commonly used for RNA-virus detection. The abbreviation RT means reverse transcription, whereas real-time describes observing amplification during the test. These are different concepts even when one test performs both.

What a PCR result can and cannot show

PCR-based methods are used to detect genetic material from pathogens, identify specific inherited DNA changes and test for defined genetic targets in crops. For example, an RT-PCR assay can detect RNA from a virus; a different PCR assay can check for a known bacterial DNA sequence. Antigen tests instead detect particular proteins, while antibody tests detect the body's immune response.

A positive PCR result shows that the assay's target genetic material was detected in the sample; it does not by itself prove that a pathogen is alive, that infection is severe or that the patient is infectious. A negative result can occur if the target is absent, present below the detection limit or missed because of sample or test limitations. Results must be interpreted with the clinical context.

Prelims focus

  • PCR stands for polymerase chain reaction.
  • PCR amplifies a selected DNA segment rather than reading its exact sequence.
  • Primers specify the target region; DNA polymerase makes copies.
  • RT-PCR includes conversion of RNA into complementary DNA.
  • Antigen, antibody and nucleic-acid tests detect different targets.
  • Trap: Reverse transcription and real-time detection are not the same meaning of RT.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, “Biotechnology: Principles and Processes”, §11.3.3 (GPSC Books vol. 35, PDF pp. 227–228); NCERT, Biology, Class 12, “Biotechnology and its Applications”, §12.2.3 (GPSC Books vol. 35, PDF p. 237); NHGRI, “Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)”, Talking Glossary, and “Understanding COVID-19 PCR Testing”, section explaining reverse transcription (consulted 5 November 2026); World Health Organization, “Transmission of SARS-CoV-2: implications for infection prevention precautions”, discussion of RNA detection and viral viability (2020).]
